description: A perennial herb about 60-100 cm tall with large lanceolate leaves rising from a short pseudostem and a branching, orange-yellow underground rhizome. Pale yellow flower spikes with pinkish bracts appear in the rainy season.
cultural_significance: Turmeric paste is applied in Hindu weddings (haldi ceremony) and offered in many rituals as an auspicious, purifying substance. Haridra is also a staple of Indian cooking and natural dyeing.
habitat: Warm, humid tropical conditions with rich, well-drained loamy soil; grown as a field crop across India.

uses.title: Wounds, skin disorders and rashes
uses.detail: Haridra is described as Varnya and Kushthaghna; paste is traditionally applied to wounds, boils and skin eruptions, and taken internally in skin disorders.

uses.title: Cough, cold and throat irritation
uses.detail: Warm milk or water with turmeric is a widely used household remedy for cough and sore throat; described as Kaphahara.

uses.title: Prameha (metabolic and urinary disorders)
uses.detail: Haridra with Amalaki is a classical combination traditionally used in Prameha, an Ayurvedic category loosely related to diabetes.

uses.title: Joint pain and inflammation
uses.detail: Traditionally used with warm oil or in decoctions for painful, swollen joints; curcumin is studied for anti-inflammatory activity.

uses.title: Digestive support
uses.detail: Used in cooking and as a mild digestive and liver-supporting spice (Deepana, Pachana).

ayurveda.vedic_note: Haridra (turmeric) is associated with early ritual and folk-medicine practice and is described in later Ayurvedic texts; I have not cited a specific Vedic verse, so treat its Vedic-era use as traditional rather than precisely sourced.

preparations.name: Haridra churna (powder)
preparations.method: Boil, dry and finely powder the rhizome.
preparations.note: Used in food, pastes and traditional formulations.

preparations.name: Lepa (external paste)
preparations.method: Mix powder with water, milk or honey to form a paste and apply on the skin.
preparations.note: Traditionally used on minor wounds and skin blemishes; patch test first.

preparations.name: Haldi doodh (golden milk)
preparations.method: Simmer a pinch of powder in milk, optionally with black pepper.
preparations.note: A common household drink during colds.

preparations.name: Kwatha (decoction)
preparations.method: Boil rhizome pieces in water, strain.
preparations.note: Used by practitioners for internal use.

precautions: Large supplement amounts may thin the blood or lower blood sugar; people on anticoagulants, antiplatelet or diabetes medicines should consult a doctor. Avoid medicinal quantities in pregnancy and with gallstones or bile duct obstruction. May upset the stomach in some people. Curcumin is poorly absorbed on its own.

cultivation.water: Regular in growing season; avoid waterlogging
cultivation.propagation: Planted from rhizome pieces (finger bulbs) at the start of the monsoon
cultivation.harvest: Harvest 7-9 months after planting when leaves yellow and dry

conservation_status: Not threatened; widely cultivated (India is the largest producer).
fun_fact: The yellow pigment curcumin is named after the plant's genus, and turmeric rhizomes are boiled before drying to give the deep colour.

regions.name: South Asia (Widely cultivated)
regions.note: Major spice crop of the subcontinent

regions.name: Deccan Plateau
regions.note: Large commercial cultivation, e.g. Sangli and Nizamabad belts

regions.name: Tamil Nadu Plains
regions.note: Erode is a well-known turmeric trading centre
